name: Luxembourg

tax_year.return_due: The return for 2026 must be filed by 31 December 2027.

summary: Gains on shares, funds and crypto held privately for more than 6 months are tax-free, unless you own more than 10% of a company. Dividends and interest are taxed at your normal progressive rates, with the first €1,500 a year tax-free and half of most company dividends exempt. Most interest paid by a Luxembourg bank instead has a final 20% tax withheld.

topics.title: Profit when you sell
points: If you hold 10% or less of a company, a gain on shares or securities sold more than 6 months after buying is tax-free.
A gain on something sold within 6 months of buying is a speculative gain, taxed at your normal progressive rates. Speculative gains are tax-free if your total for the year is less than €500.
Different rules apply if you held more than 10% of a company at any time in the last 5 years.
Taxable gains go in the return as miscellaneous income (revenus nets divers), with details of each sale.

topics.title: Dividends
points: Dividends are added to your income and taxed at your normal progressive rates, plus the 1.4% dependency insurance contribution.
Half of a dividend is tax-free if it comes from a fully taxable capital company (such as an SA or SARL) in Luxembourg, another EU country or a country with a tax treaty with Luxembourg.
Luxembourg companies withhold 15% tax on dividends. In principle it is credited against your income tax in the return.

topics.title: Interest on savings
points: Most interest paid by a Luxembourg bank has a final 20% tax withheld (retenue à la source libératoire, RELIBI). You do not declare that interest, and the tax cannot be refunded or credited.
This applies, for example, to savings and term deposits when the interest is more than €250 a year per person and per bank, and to current accounts paying more than 0.75% a year.

Interest from a bank abroad is taxed at your progressive rates. If the bank is in the EU or EEA, you can instead choose the final 20% tax on all such interest by filing form 931 by 31 December of the following year.

topics.title: Tax on what you own
points: Luxembourg abolished wealth tax for private individuals, in the same law that introduced the 20% final tax on interest.

topics.title: Tax-free amounts
points: The first €1,500 a year of taxable interest and dividends is tax-free, or €3,000 for spouses or partners taxed together.
You can deduct a flat €25 a year in costs (€50 for couples taxed together), or your real costs if higher.
Speculative gains of less than €500 in total for the year are tax-free.

topics.title: Tax-free and tax-deferred accounts
points: Payments into a pension saving contract (prévoyance-vieillesse) can be deducted from taxable income, up to €4,500 a year from the 2026 tax year (it was €3,200 up to 2025). Spouses with their own contracts each have this limit.

topics.title: Losses
points: Losses on sales can be set against gains, but not against other kinds of income, and they cannot be carried to later years.

topics.title: Foreign shares
points: Tax withheld abroad on dividends is in principle credited against Luxembourg income tax. If it cannot all be credited, the rest can be deducted as a cost.
Foreign withholding tax on interest can be credited where a tax treaty allows it.
Dividends from foreign companies in treaty countries are reported on annex 180 of the return.

topics.title: What your broker does and what you do
points: A Luxembourg bank withholds the final 20% on interest, and Luxembourg companies withhold 15% on their dividends. You still declare dividends in your return, using the certificate from your bank.
A foreign bank or broker does not apply the final 20% tax on interest. You declare dividends, interest and any taxable gains from it in your return.

topics.title: Crypto
points: Exchanging crypto, including for another crypto, counts as selling it. A gain or loss within 6 months of buying is speculative and taxed at your progressive rates.
Speculative gains are tax-free if your total for the year is less than €500.

dates.what: Deadline for the return for the year before, and for choosing the final 20% tax on foreign interest (form 931).

not_covered: Investment funds in detail, including whether fund distributions get the 50% dividend exemption.
Holdings of more than 10% in one company.
Non-residents and cross-border workers, including the option to be taxed as a resident.
